The date included the election of the [[Governor of Maryland|governor]], [[Lieutenant Governor of Maryland|lieutenant governor]], and all members of the [[Maryland General Assembly]]. Popular incumbent Governor [[Larry Hogan]] and Lieutenant Governor [[Boyd Rutherford]], both [[Maryland Republican Party|Republicans]], were elected to a second term in a landslide against Democrat [[Ben Jealous]], the former [[NAACP]] CEO, and his running mate [[Susan Turnbull]]. This was one of eight Republican-held governorships up for election in a state carried by [[Hillary Clinton]] in the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 presidential election]]. Hogan became the second Republican governor of Maryland to win re-election, and the first since [[Theodore McKeldin]] in [[1954 Maryland gubernatorial election|1954]].{{cite news |url=https://www.wbaltv.com/article/hogan-becomes-first-gop-governor-to-win-second-term-in-maryland-since-1954/24510818 |title=Gov. Larry Hogan makes history with re-election in Maryland |first1=Greg |last1=Ng |publisher=[[WBAL-TV]] |date=November 6, 2018 |first2=Kate |last2=Amara |access-date=November 7, 2018}} He also became the first Republican to win over 55% of the vote in a statewide election in Maryland since U.S. Senator [[Charles Mathias]] in [[1980 United States Senate election in Maryland|1980]]. This was the first election since 1974 in which Maryland simultaneously elected a gubernatorial nominee and a U.S. Senate nominee of opposite parties. This was the first and only Maryland gubernatorial election in which both major party candidates received over one million votes. As of 2025, this is the last time that a Republican won a statewide election in Maryland. ==Background== At the presidential level, [[Maryland]] is a staunchly Democratic state due to the large number of Democratic voters in the [[Washington metropolitan area]] and [[Baltimore]] City. Maryland had not seen a Republican presidential candidate win its votes since 1988, and the state had not been within 15% since [[2004 United States presidential election in Maryland|2004]]; [[Hillary Clinton]] won the state by 26 points over [[Donald Trump]] (60% to 34%) in 2016, [[Barack Obama]] defeated [[Mitt Romney]] by 26 points in 2012 (62% to 36%), and Obama defeated [[John McCain]] by 25 points in 2008 (62% to 37%). Hogan was elected governor in [[2014 Maryland gubernatorial election|2014]], defeating then-lieutenant governor [[Anthony Brown (Maryland politician)|Anthony Brown]] by a margin of 51% to 47%; the result was considered one of the biggest election upsets that year.{{Cite web |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/md-politics/republican-larry-hogan-wins-md-governors-race-in-stunning-upset/2014/11/05/9eb8bf46-60ac-11e4-8b9e-2ccdac31a031_story.html |title=Republican Larry Hogan wins Md. governor's race in stunning upset |access-date=2018-08-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180803154213/https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/md-politics/republican-larry-hogan-wins-md-governors-race-in-stunning-upset/2014/11/05/9eb8bf46-60ac-11e4-8b9e-2ccdac31a031_story.html |archive-date=2018-08-03 |url-status=live |date=November 5, 2014 |newspaper=The Washington Post |first1=John |last1=Wagner |first2=Jenna |last2=Johnson }} Prior to Hogan's victory, [[Bob Ehrlich]], elected in [[2002 Maryland gubernatorial election|2002]], had been the only Republican elected as Governor of Maryland since [[Spiro Agnew]]. However, Ehrlich was defeated for reelection in [[2006 Maryland gubernatorial election|2006]] by [[Martin O'Malley]] and defeated again in [[2010 Maryland gubernatorial election|2010]], when he faced O'Malley in a rematch.
